title: Right Action and Right Livelihood
originalTitle: Bhante G - Right Action & Right Livelihood
brief: Our actions and work affect both the mind and the wider community. Bhante G places right action and right livelihood within the whole Noble Eightfold Path, emphasizing intention, conscience, honesty, and the consequences of harm. He discusses killing, stealing, misuse of the senses, harmful trades, and the responsibilities of monastics who depend on others. A difficult example considers livelihood when someone truly has no alternative way to support a family; it is a qualified discussion, not a general approval of harmful work. Earning a fair profit is compatible with practice. Deception and exploitation undermine the peace that meditation requires.
summaryMarkdown:
## Two factors within one connected path

Right action and right livelihood support the other factors of the Noble Eightfold Path and are supported by them. Bhante G compares the path to a complete, unbroken circle. Understanding and intention inform conduct; conduct affects effort, mindfulness, and concentration.

These practices are therefore not merely social rules. What we do to others shapes the condition of our own minds and the society in which we live.

## Intention and conscience

Right action includes abstaining from killing, stealing, and misconduct involving the senses. Bhante G examines the conditions of intentional killing and stresses intention as essential. His example of an accidentally thrown stone killing an unseen animal distinguishes an unintended result from an intention to kill.

His self-defense example likewise concerns an unintended death in a situation in which the person had no intention to kill. The emphasis remains honest examination of intention and conscience.

Likewise, stolen property placed in front of an innocent person does not establish that the person stole it. An intention to take what belongs to another cannot be hidden from one's own conscience, even if other people do not discover the act. Bhante G repeatedly asks listeners to be honest with themselves.

He also describes restraint in the use of eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind. The ethical training extends beyond a single bodily act to the ways one encourages or restrains harmful states.

## How livelihood affects others

A job is not isolated from its consequences. Bhante G discusses harmful trades involving weapons, living beings and slavery, meat, and poison. He asks listeners to consider what their work produces and how it affects people, animals, and the environment.

Work that repeatedly brings harm also affects meditation. Remembering one's harmful actions can disturb the mind when trying to settle it. Choosing a livelihood calls for conscience and attention to consequences, not merely the question of whether it provides income.

## A qualified discussion of necessity

Bhante G considers a difficult situation: someone has family responsibilities, no land or other skill, no alternative employment, and only a factory job available. In that specific context, he says the person's intention to maintain a living, rather than to poison or harm, must be considered. He gives a related example involving work whose final products become government weapons.

This is a qualification within his discussion of intention and necessity. It does not erase his earlier advice to avoid harmful trades when choosing one's work, nor does it establish that any job becomes harmless merely because it earns a living.

## Monastic livelihood

Monastics also need food and other requisites. They should receive support without deception or overburdening households. Bhante G uses the image of a bee gathering nectar without damaging the flower. Receiving modest offerings from several homes differs from taking so much that one family is deprived.

He cautions monastics against obtaining support through activities such as fortune-telling and acting as marriage brokers. Their means of support should strengthen confidence and generosity rather than exploit the people who provide it.

## Honest profit and generosity

Bhante G does not condemn business, profit, or household responsibility. Profit may provide for living expenses, overhead, reinvestment, and future needs. The problem is deceptive dealing or taking an unfair advantage. He also recalls a division of earnings: one portion for daily living, two for investment, and one saved for future difficulties.

The closing story contrasts two traders encountering a poor family with an unrecognized gold plate. One trader conceals its value and plans to obtain it cheaply. The honest trader acknowledges its worth and gives what he can in exchange. The dishonest trader's greed becomes his own ruin. The story gathers the talk's themes: livelihood should be examined through honesty, intention, fairness, and its effect on others and oneself.
